Unit 1: Grammar Homework
Section 1. Verb Forms and Their Derivatives
Task 1: Identifying Verbs
Read the paragraph below and underline all action verbs, linking verbs, auxiliary verbs, and modal verbs. Then, sort each verb into the table provided.
"Sarah can play the piano beautifully. She has been practicing every day because she wants to improve. Her teacher told her that she should focus on her timing and rhythm. If she continues to practice diligently, she will become an excellent pianist."

Task 2: Word Formation
Convert the following verbs into their noun forms (gerunds, agent nouns, action nouns) and adjective forms (present participle, past participle, adjective-forming suffixes).

Task 3: Writing Sentences
Write five sentences using at least one modal verb and one auxiliary verb in each sentence.
Example: She must have finished her homework before going to bed.
The environment should be protected
She might have gone to picnic if it hadn’t rained
We will have learned a lot by the end of the course
If the bus hadn’t arrived late I wouldn’t have missed the meeting
If i had tried harder, i could have passed the exam
Section 2. Prepositions and Pronouns
Task 1: Filling in Prepositions
Choose the correct preposition (in, on, at) for each sentence.
We have a meeting on__ Monday morning.
My keys are _on__ the table.
I was born _in__ 1995.
She lives _in__ a small apartment.
The book is _on__ the shelf.
Task 2: Replacing Nouns with Pronouns
Rewrite the sentences below, replacing the nouns with the correct pronouns.
John gave the book to Mary.
-> John gave the book to her
The students are doing their homework.
-> They are doing their homework
My brother and I went to the store.
-> He and I went to the store
Sarah loves her new dress.
-> she loves her new dress
The cat is sleeping on the sofa.
-> it is sleeping on the sofa
Task 3: Identifying Pronoun References
Read the passage below and underline all the pronouns. Then, write down the noun each pronoun refers to.
Passage: "Mike went to the grocery store because he needed some vegetables. When he arrived, he saw Anna. She was buying fruits for her family. Mike helped her carry the bags."

3. Phrases and Sentence Structure
Task 1: Expanding Phrases
Take the basic phrases below and expand them using adjectives, adverbs, and relative clauses.
Example: A beautiful morning → A very beautiful, sunny morning when I was walking with my brother.
Now, expand these phrases:
A big house -> a extremely big,beautiful house which was built in 2020
A delicious meal → an excessively delicious, luxurious meal that is suitable for the rich
A small puppy → a really cute,small puppy that i very love
A friendly neighbor →a very friendly,kind neighbor who is a teacher in my school
A rainy day -> a rainy, boring day that i don’t want to hang out
Task 2: Breaking Down and Rebuilding Sentences
Analyze the structure of these complex sentences by identifying the subject, verb, object, and phrases. Then, rewrite them in a different way while keeping their meaning intact.
Example: Original: The little boy who lives next door is playing in the garden. Breakdown:
Subject: The little boy
Relative Clause: who lives next door
Verb: is playing
Prepositional Phrase: in the garden
Rewritten: The little boy is playing in the garden. He lives next door.
Now, complete this task with the following sentences:
The woman who helped me yesterday works in a bank.
-> the woman works in a bank. She helped me yesterday
The cake that my mother baked was delicious.
-> the cake was delicious. My mother baked it
The car that he bought last week is very expensive.
0-> the car is very expensive .He bought it last week
4. Real-World Practice: Writing About Your Dream City
Write a short paragraph (5-7 sentences) about your dream city. Use different types of verbs (action, auxiliary, modal), prepositions, and well-structured phrases.
Example: My dream city is located on a beautiful island. It has modern skyscrapers and green parks. People can enjoy their time at the beach or visit historical landmarks. There are many cozy cafés where you can relax and read. The transportation system is very efficient, making it easy to explore every corner of the city.
Now, write your own paragraph
My dream city is a place with a lot of advanced technology. It has a considerable number of modern constructions and high-rise buildings.City dwellers can go around the city by a cutting-edge car which is very fast and eco-friendly. Therefore, exploring every corner of the city is really easy for inhabitants.Beside, there are aa variety of means of entertainment such as cozy cafe or cinema where you can relax after the stressful time at school or work.

Task 1A Script: Customer Service Call
"Good afternoon! Can I have your full name, please?"
"Yes, it's Emily Barclay."
"Thank you, could you spell that out for me?"
"Sure! E-M-I-L-Y for my first name, and B-A-R-C-L-A-Y for my last name."
"Perfect. Now, can I have your phone number?"
"Yes, it's (415) 762-8391."
"That’s four-one-five, seven-six-two, eight-three-nine-one?"
"Yes, that’s correct."
"Great! Lastly, I need to provide you with a tracking number for your package. It is 392-5714-86. Could you read that back to me?"
"Certainly! Three-nine-two, five-seven-one-four, eight-six."
"Excellent! Your package is expected to arrive on April 15th. Thank you for confirming your details!"
Task 1B Script: Flight Booking Information
"Good morning! I need to confirm some details for your booking. Could you please tell me your full name?"
"Yes, it’s Monique Xu."
"Can you spell that out for me?"
"Sure! M-O-N-I-Q-U-E for my first name, and X-U for my last name."
"Got it. Now, I see that you’re flying from Newark to Sydney. Could you confirm the departure city?"
"Yes, that’s Newark."
"Just to be sure, is that spelled N-E-W-A-R-K?"
"Yes, that’s correct."
"Great! Now, let’s review your travel dates. Your departure is on March 15th, and you’ll return on April 5th, 2025. Is that right?"
"Yes, March 15th to April 5th, 2025."
"Perfect. Now, regarding the total payment, the amount due is twelve hundred dollars."
"Sorry, did you say twelve hundred or one thousand two hundred?"
"It’s the same thing—twelve hundred dollars means one thousand two hundred dollars."
"Ah, I see!"
"And your confirmation number is WU-509-XA15. Could you read that back to me?"
"Yes, it’s WU-509-XA15."
"Excellent! Your ticket details have been confirmed. You’ll receive an email shortly. Have a great day!"
Task 2A Script: Polar Bears at the Zoo
"Good afternoon, everyone! Welcome to the Arctic section of the zoo. Today, we’ll be talking about one of the most fascinating animals in the world—the polar bear."
"Oh, I love polar bears! They look so cute and fluffy."
"They do, don’t they? But don’t let their cuddly appearance fool you—they are powerful hunters. Polar bears are native to the Arctic region and are perfectly adapted to live in freezing temperatures. Their thick fur and a layer of blubber help them stay warm."
"I heard their fur is actually not white. Is that true?"
"Yes, that’s correct! Their fur appears white, but it’s actually transparent. It reflects light, which helps them blend into their snowy surroundings. Underneath, their skin is actually black, which helps absorb heat from the sun."
"Wow! What do they usually eat in the wild?"
"Their main diet consists of seals, but they also eat fish when necessary. They are expert hunters and can detect seals from miles away. However, due to climate change, polar bears are struggling to find food because they are losing their sea ice, which they rely on for hunting."
"That’s sad. So, do they hibernate in the winter like other bears?"
"That’s a great question! Unlike other bear species, polar bears do not hibernate. The only ones that stay in dens for long periods are pregnant females."
"And how big do they get?"
"A fully grown male can weigh up to 700 kilograms! That’s almost the same weight as a small car. They are also excellent swimmers and can swim long distances between ice sheets."
"What do they eat here at the zoo?"
"At the zoo, we try to mimic their natural diet by feeding them a special meal plan that includes fish, meat, and vitamins to keep them healthy."
"That’s really interesting. Thank you for all the information!"
"You’re welcome! If you’d like, you can stay and watch our feeding session in about 15 minutes."
Task 2B Script: The Oak Tree Talk
"Welcome to our nature walk! Today, we’ll be learning about one of the most important trees in this forest—the oak tree."
"I’ve heard that oak trees live a really long time."
"That’s right! Some oak trees can live for over 1,000 years. In fact, the oldest oak tree in the world is estimated to be around 1,500 years old!"
"That’s amazing. What do their leaves look like?"
"Oak leaves are typically lobed, which means they have rounded edges. In autumn, they turn beautiful shades of red and orange before falling off."
"I know oak trees produce acorns, but what exactly are they?"
"Acorns are the fruit of the oak tree. Many animals, including squirrels and deer, rely on them for food. You might see some animals collecting them as we walk."
"What is oak wood used for?"
"Oak wood is known for being very strong, so it's often used in furniture and construction. It’s also resistant to pests, which makes it even more valuable."
"How tall can these trees get?"
"Some oak trees can grow up to 40 meters tall! They also have wide root systems that help them absorb water and stay strong against storms."
"I’ve heard that oak trees have symbolic meanings in different cultures."
"That’s true! Many cultures see the oak tree as a symbol of strength and wisdom. In ancient times, people believed oak trees were sacred and even held ceremonies under their branches."
"That’s really interesting. Thank you for sharing all this information!"
"You’re welcome! Let’s keep walking, and I’ll point out a few more interesting trees along the way."

Answer Key: Reading Homework Assignment
Task 1: Recognizing Verbs and Their Derivatives
**Identified Verbs in the Excerpt:**
living, have, get, required, have, treated, might, be, restricted, live, aid, are, becoming, threatened, risk
Adj: varied, safe // Adv: increasingly 
Noun: movement, conservation, extinction, supplements, life, illnesses
**Converted Verbs into Different Forms:**
- Verb: restrict → Noun: restriction, Adjective: restrictive, Participle: restricted
- Verb: threaten → Noun: threat, Adjective: threatening, Participle: threatened
- Verb: require → Noun: requirement, Adjective: required, Participle: required
- Verb: aid → Noun: aid, Adjective: aiding, Participle: aided
Task 2: Recognizing Referencing and Substituting Devices
**Referencing Devices Identified:**
- Especially those in cities = Many children and adults
- That alone (demonstrative reference) = seeing a living creature
- them, they (last sentence) (pronoun referring to 'children and adults')
- hearing it, smelling it, watching what it does (pronoun IT referring to ‘a living creature’)
**Substituting Devices Identified:**
- will bring a greater understanding and perspective to many = many people (children and adult)
- Natural history specimens (substituting 'museum exhibits')
- Conservation efforts (substituting 'wildlife preservation initiatives')
**Sentence Rewrite Example:**
Original: 'That alone will bring a greater understanding and perspective to many, and hopefully give them a greater appreciation for wildlife, conservation efforts and how they can contribute.'
Rewritten: 'Seeing a living creature in the flesh will bring a greater understanding and perspective to many people, and hopefully give children and adults a greater appreciation for wildlife, conservation efforts, and how people can contribute.'
Task 3: Identifying Parts of Speech & Summarization
**Identified Parts of Speech:**
- Adjectives: wild, real
- Adverbs: also, really
- Prepositional phrases: 'on animals in zoos,' 'of its breeding rate'
- Examples: 'the oestrus cycle,' ‘such as capturing and moving at-risk or dangerous individuals’
**Summarized Passage:**
Original: 'Zoos also play a key role in research... [full excerpt]...'
Summarized Version: 'Zoos contribute to research by providing controlled environments to study animal behavior, reproduction, and conservation techniques, which helps manage wild populations and reduce human-animal conflicts.'

Unit 1 Reading Homework: Recognizing Language Features in Text + Practice Scanning Skill
Objective:
This assignment helps students practice four key reading skills:
1. Identifying verbs and their derivatives (nouns, adjectives, participles).
2. Recognizing referencing and substituting devices.
3. Identifying different parts of speech to summarize text effectively.
4. Understanding how sentence structure affects clarity and conciseness.
(All excerpts taken from Cambridge Reading Test 14.4)
Task 1: Recognizing Verbs and Their Derivatives
Read the following excerpt from the text and underline all the verbs. Then, classify them into their different forms (base verb, noun, adjective, or participle).
"In my view, it is perfectly possible for many species of animals living in zoos or wildlife parks to have a quality of life as high as, or higher than, in the wild. Animals in good zoos get a varied and high-quality diet with all the supplements required, and any illnesses they might have will be treated. Their movement might be somewhat restricted, but they have a safe environment in which to live. Zoos aid conservation. Colossal numbers of species are becoming extinct across the world, and many more are increasingly threatened and therefore risk extinction."
Identify all the Verbs in the excerpt (underline them)
Convert 5 Verbs into their Adj or Noun forms
Identify Adjectives + Adverbs that are derived from verbs. (underline them)
Identify Nouns that are derived from verbs. (underline them)
Create five new sentences using the verbs and their derivatives in different forms.
Example Answer:
- Verb: protect → Noun: protection, Adjective: protective, Participle: protected
Task 2: Recognizing Referencing and Substituting Devices
Read the excerpt below and highlight words or phrases that act as referencing (pronouns, demonstratives) or substituting devices (synonyms, paraphrasing).
"Zoos also provide education. Many children and adults, especially those in cities, will never see a wild animal beyond a fox or pigeon. While it is true that television documentaries are becoming ever more detailed and impressive, and many natural history specimens are on display in museums, there really is nothing to compare with seeing a living creature in the flesh, hearing it, smelling it, watching what it does and having the time to absorb details. That alone will bring a greater understanding and perspective to many, and hopefully give them a greater appreciation for wildlife, conservation efforts and how they can contribute."
1. Identify three words/phrases that act as referencing devices (e.g., pronouns, demonstratives like 'this,' 'that,' etc.) and point out what word they are referencing to.
2. Identify three words/phrases that act as substituting devices (words that avoid repetition by using synonyms/ quantifiers) and point out what word they are substituting for.
3. Rewrite one sentence from the text replacing a referencing or substituting device with its full noun phrase.
4. Write three sentences of your own that use referencing and substituting devices effectively.
Task 3: Identifying Parts of Speech & Summarization
Read the excerpt below and identify different parts of speech. Then, shorten the text by removing unnecessary elements like adverbs, adjectives, prepositional phrases, or examples while keeping the meaning intact.
"Zoos also play a key role in research. If we are to save wild species and restore and repair ecosystems, we need to know about how key species live, act and react. Being able to undertake research on animals in zoos where there is less risk and fewer variables means real changes can be effected on wild populations. Finding out about, for example, the oestrus cycle of an animal of its breeding rate helps us manage wild populations. Procedures such as capturing and moving at-risk or dangerous individuals are bolstered by knowledge gained in zoos about doses for anaesthetics, and by experience in handling and transporting animals. This can make a real difference to conservation efforts and to the reduction of human-animal conflicts, and can provide a knowledge base for helping with the increasing threats of habitat destruction and other problems."
1. Identify two adjectives, two adverbs, two prepositional phrases, and two examples in the text.
2. Shorten each sentence in the text by removing unnecessary elements while keeping the main message.
3. Write 2 sentences that summarize the main idea of the paragraph.

IELTS Speaking Homework Assignment
Objective:
This assignment will help you strengthen your IELTS Speaking skills by practicing fluency, coherence, pronunciation, vocabulary, and grammatical range & accuracy. You will apply what you have learned about structured responses in Speaking Part 1 and record your answers for review. Additionally, you will focus on improving your confidence in speaking spontaneously and refining your ability to extend answers naturally. This practice will help you develop a strong speaking habit that aligns with IELTS marking criteria.
Part 1: Speaking Skill Reinforcement
A. Key Speaking Strategies (Slides 49-56 Review)
Before answering, remember these essential rules for IELTS Speaking Part 1:
Keep your answers within 2-3 sentences and ensure clarity.
Use full sentences
Expand your answers with relevant examples, experiences, or reasoning.
Don't forget to say "yes" or "no" when necessary, then explain why.
Pay attention to intonation, rhythm, and pronunciation for clear delivery.
Avoid excessive fillers like "um," "uh," or "you know" to maintain fluency.
Part 2: Answering IELTS Speaking Part 1 Questions
Instructions:
Write down some notes (don’t write full answer) to answer the following IELTS Speaking Part 1 questions using the I-E Structure (Idea-Example/Explaination):
Keep your responses clear, well-structured, and natural.
Topic 1: Hometown
Where is your hometown?
What do you like about your hometown?
Has your hometown changed much in recent years?
Would you prefer to live in your hometown in the future? Why or why not?
What is a famous landmark or attraction in your hometown?
Topic 2: The Environment
Do you think pollution is a problem in your country?
What can individuals do to help the environment?
Have you ever participated in any environmental activities?
What are some ways schools can promote environmental awareness?
How has climate change affected your country in recent years?
Topic 3: Animals/ Plants and Zoo
Based on Listening Homework (Polar Bears & Oak Trees):
11. Have you seen any polar bears on TV?
12. What do you know about oak trees?
13. Do you usually watch TV programs about endangered animals?
14. Are there a lot of trees around your house?
Based on Reading Homework (Zoos & Conservation):
16. Have you ever been to a zoo?
17. Did you like going to the zoo when you were a child?
18. Do you love wild animals?
19. Is there any zoo in your city?
Part 3: Recording Task
Instructions:
Record yourself answering all the questions above, using the notes you have already prepared.
Speak clearly and confidently, avoiding unnecessary pauses or hesitations.
Submit your audio file before the deadline.
Listen to your recording and assess how natural and fluent your responses sound.
Self-Evaluation Checklist:
Did I answer in full sentences with clarity?
Did I keep my response concise (2-3 sentences per question) while giving enough detail?
Did I use a range of vocabulary and grammar structures to demonstrate linguistic variety?
Was my pronunciation, intonation, and fluency natural and easy to understand?
Did I avoid long pauses, excessive fillers, or repetitive phrases?
Did I structure my answers logically and confidently?
Did I use relevant examples or explanations to support my answers?
By completing this assignment, you will develop greater confidence in speaking fluently and naturally, ensuring a better performance in the IELTS Speaking test.

sections.title: Passage: How Bad Is Ocean Garbage, Really? (Cam 14.4 Passage 3)

blocks.text:
Source: Cam 14.4 Passage 3 | https://ieltstrainingonline.com/practice-cam-14-reading-test-04-with-answer/

Chelsea Rochman, an ecologist at the University of California, Davis, has been trying to answer a dismal question: Is everything terrible, or are things just very, very bad?

Rochman is a member of the National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis’s marine-debris working group, a collection of scientists who study, among other things, the growing problem of marine debris, also known as ocean trash. Plenty of studies have sounded alarm bells about the state of marine debris; in a recent paper published in the journal Ecology, Rochman and her colleagues set out to determine how many of those perceived risks are real.

Often, Rochman says, scientists will end a paper by speculating about the broader impacts of what they’ve found. For example, a study could show that certain seabirds eat plastic bags, and go on to warn that whole bird populations are at risk of dying out. ‘But the truth was that nobody had yet tested those perceived threats,’ Rochman says. ‘There wasn’t a lot of information.’

Rochman and her colleagues examined more than a hundred papers on the impacts of marine debris that were published through 2013. Within each paper, they asked what threats scientists had studied – 366 perceived threats in all – and what they’d actually found.

In 83 percent of cases, the perceived dangers of ocean trash were proven true. In the remaining cases, the working group found the studies had weaknesses in design and content which affected the validity of their conclusions – they lacked a control group, for example, or used faulty statistics.

Strikingly, Rochman says, only one well-designed study failed to find the effect it was looking for, an investigation of mussels ingesting microscopic bits. The plastic moved from the mussels’ stomachs to their bloodstreams, scientists found, and stayed there for weeks – but didn’t seem to stress out the shellfish.

While mussels may be fine eating trash, though, the analysis also gave a clearer picture of the many ways that ocean debris is bothersome.

Within the studies they looked at, most of the proven threats came from plastic debris, rather than other materials like metal or wood. Most of the dangers also involved large pieces of debris – animals getting entangled in trash, for example, or eating it and severely injuring themselves.

But a lot of ocean debris is ‘microplastic’, or pieces smaller than five millimeters. These may be ingredients used in cosmetics and toiletries, fibers shed by synthetic clothing in the wash, or eroded remnants of larger debris. Compared to the number of studies investigating large-scale debris, Rochman’s group found little research on the effects of these tiny bits. ‘There are a lot of open questions still for microplastic,’ Rochman says, though she notes that more papers on the subject have been published since 2013, the cutoff point for the group’s analysis.

There are also, she adds, a lot of open questions about the ways that ocean debris can lead to sea-creature death. Many studies have looked at how plastic affects an individual animal, or that animal’s tissues or cells, rather than whole populations. And in the lab, scientists often use higher concentrations of plastic than what’s really in the ocean. None of that tells us how many birds or fish or sea turtles could die from plastic pollution – or how deaths in one species could affect that animal’s predators, or the rest of the ecosystem.

‘We need to be asking more ecologically relevant questions,’ Rochman says. Usually, scientists don’t know exactly how disasters such as a tanker accidentally spilling its whole cargo of oil and polluting huge areas of the ocean will affect the environment until after they’ve happened. ‘We don’t ask the right questions early enough,’ she says. But if ecologists can understand how the slow-moving effect of ocean trash is damaging ecosystems, they might be able to prevent things from getting worse.

Asking the right questions can help policy makers, and the public, figure out where to focus their attention. The problems that look or sound most dramatic may not be the best places to start. For example, the name of the ‘Great Pacific Garbage Patch’ – a collection of marine debris in the northern Pacific Ocean – might conjure up a vast, floating trash island. In reality though, much of the debris is tiny or below the surface; a person could sail through the area without seeing any trash at all. A Dutch group called ‘The Ocean Cleanup’ is currently working on plans to put mechanical devices in the Pacific Garbage Patch and similar areas to suck up plastic. But a recent paper used simulations to show that strategically positioning the cleanup devices closer to shore would more effectively reduce pollution over the long term.

‘I think clearing up some of these misperceptions is really important,’ Rochman says. Among scientists as well as in the media, she says, ‘A lot of the images about strandings and entanglement and all of that cause the perception that plastic debris is killing everything in the ocean.’ Interrogating the existing scientific literature can help ecologists figure out which problems really need addressing, and which ones they’d be better off – like the mussels – absorbing and ignoring.

Types of words in English
Nouns: describe objects/ events.
Pronouns: a type of Noun that refers to Objects that are mentioned before.
Verbs: describe actions.
Adjectives: describe qualities/features of Nouns.
Adverbs: describe qualities/features of Verbs/ Adjectives/ other Adverbs.
Preposition: function words that stand before a Noun that denote position/ time
Articles: a/an/the – function words denoting the specificity of a Noun

Verbs and their derivatives:
The Basic Form of Verb:
Action verbs: Show physical or mental action (e.g., run, think, write).
Linking verbs: Connect the subject to a subject complement (e.g., be, seem, become).
Auxiliary (Helping) verbs: Help the main verb form tenses, voices, or moods (e.g., have, do, will).
Modal verbs: Express possibility, necessity, or permission (e.g., can, must, should).

Verbs and their derivatives:
Verb to Noun Forms:
Gerunds (-ing form as a noun): Swimming is fun. (swim → swimming)
Agent nouns (-er, -ant, -ist): A teacher educates. (teach → teacher)
Action nouns (-tion, -sion, -ment, -ance, -ence): His swift decision on this matter must be difficult. (decide → decision)Compare: Deciding swiftly on this matter must be difficult for him.

Verbs and their derivatives:
Verb to Adjective Forms:
Present participles (-ing): The running water is cold. (run → running) (active)
Past participles (-ed, -en, -t, etc.): A broken vase. (break → broken) (passive)
Adjective-forming suffixes (-able, -ive, -ous, -al):
This task is doable. (do → doable)
He is creative. (create → creative)

Preposition: in, on, at
IN
Enclosed spaces, countries, and large areas
She is in the school
Months, years, centuries, and long periods
I was born in July.
ON
Surfaces, Specific Dates, and Devices
The book is on the table.
Specific days and dates
They arrived on Christmas Day.
AT
Specific Points and Exact Times
We are at the bus stop.
The train arrives at 5 PM.

Pronouns: Referencing Devices
Referencing: nhắc đến thứ ở phía trước
Personal pronouns (he, she, we, you,…)
John is my best friend. He is very kind.
I love this book. It is interesting.
Demonstrative pronouns(this, that, these, those, the)
Look at this! (something nearby)
I read a great book last week. That was amazing.
Comparative Reference(same, different, more, less, better)
She bought a dress. I bought the same one.
This house is bigger than the other one

Pronouns: Substituting Devices
Substituting: thay thế từ/ vế câu phía trước
Noun Substitution (one(s), the same)
I need a pen. Do you have one?
He ordered tea, and I ordered the same.
Verbal Substitution (do, does, did, so, or same)
She sings beautifully. I wish I could do that!
He worked hard, and she did too.
Clause/Sentence Substitution (so, not, or that)
Will it rain today? I hope the same.
Do you think he will come? I don’t think so.

PHRASES:
In English grammar, phrases are groups of words that function as a single unit in a sentence.

Types of phrases
A noun phrase consists of a noun and other words that describe or modify the noun.
For example, "the big red apple" is a noun phrase, where "apple" is the noun and "big" and "red" are adjectives that modify the noun.
Noun Phrase:
An adjective phrase consists of an adjective and other words that modify the adjective.
For example, "very happy" is an adjective phrase, where "happy" is the adjective and "very" is an adverb that modifies the adjective.
Adjective Phrase:
An adverb phrase consists of an adverb and other words that modify the verb, adjective, or other adverb.
For example, "quite slowly" is an adverb phrase, where "slowly" is the adverb and "quite" is an adverb that modifies the adverb.
Adverb Phrase:
A prepositional phrase consists of a preposition, its object, and any modifiers of the object.
For example, "on the table" is a prepositional phrase, where "on" is the preposition and "the table" is the object.
Prepositional Phrase:

Types of Verb-phrases
An infinitive phrase consists of an infinitive verb (to + verb) and any modifiers of the infinitive.
For example, "to go to the store" is an infinitive phrase, where "to go" is the infinitive verb and "to the store" is a prepositional phrase that modifies the infinitive.
Infinitive Phrase:
A gerund phrase consists of a gerund (verb + -ing) and any modifiers of the gerund.
For example, "swimming in the pool" is a gerund phrase, where "swimming" is the gerund and "in the pool" is a prepositional phrase that modifies the gerund.
Gerund Phrase:
A participial phrase consists of a participle (verb + -ed or -ing) and any modifiers of the participle.
For example, "running down the street" is a participial phrase, where "running" is the present participle and "down the street" is a prepositional phrase that modifies the participle.

a process that your brain intuitively/ subconsciously performs when listening.

Familiarize with the IELTS Speaking Test + Marking Criteria
Part 1 I-E Development

The IELTS Speaking Test Format
Part 1: Introduction
4–5 minutes
general questions about yourself and familiar topics
Part 2: Long Turn
1 minute to prepare
Must speak for 1–2 minutes
Part 3: Discussion
4–5 minutes
Deeper discussion on topics from Part 2.

IELTS Speaking Marking Criteria
Fluency & Coherence
Speak smoothly without long pauses or hesitation.
Organize ideas logically and use linking words
Avoid repetition
Lexical Resource (Vocabulary)
Use various words appropriately.
Show knowledge of idioms, collocations, and paraphrasing.
Avoid overusing basic words.
Grammatical Range & Accuracy
Use varied sentence structures (simple, complex, conditional, passive, etc.).
Make minimal grammar mistakes (verb tense, prepositions, subject-verb agreement).
Use different tenses accurately (past, present, future).
Pronunciation
Speak clearly with correct word stress and intonation.
Avoid mispronouncing key words.
Be understandable.

Part 1 Development: I – E Structure

Information

Part 1 Tip: Focus on Fluency
Why? Because you can’t get a high score from part 1, so don’t try to show off your best vocabulary and get lost or make unnecessary mistakes while thinking too much for a “glowing” answer.
Follow 4 simple rules:
Keep your answers within 2 – 3 sentences.
Answer the questions using full sentences.
Expand your answer
Don't forget to say "yes" or "no" when necessary.
